rationale: A wins because it knows how to be sharp without spending facts it does not have. Its paywall angle asks for proof on "Whether existing cover owners need new hardware, the top tier, or both"; B turns that missing proof into "charging recurring fees to unlock capabilities the buyer's device already physically has." That is the difference between a pitchable tension and an unearned accusation wearing a blazer.
gaps_in_A: "A sleep clinic agreed to study a consumer mattress. Here is what it is measuring." promises more specificity than the update supplies; A mostly repairs this by saying the angle is thin until the clinic speaks.
"Decay: month" on the clinic angle is generous. With an ongoing study and no results, the launch is the only real peg unless the investigator and protocol are available.
"The company markets to athletes and biohackers" appears under the detect-and-respond facts, but the angle never fully resolves whether that audience actually cares about snoring and SpO2.
gaps_in_B: "charging recurring fees to unlock capabilities the buyer's device already physically has" is not in the update. B asks for confirmation later, but the angle has already made the accusation.

"the protagonist is the existing owner being asked to pay again" invents an existing-owner conflict. The facts say premium product and top-tier gating, not that current owners already have the sensors.

"reacts to snoring by changing the bed's temperature" overstates the mechanism. The update says the bed tracks SpO2/snoring and adjusts temperature automatically; it does not prove a snoring-triggered intervention.
"under the FDA wellness exemption" adds a specific regulatory frame not provided in the update. Useful instinct, but it needs sourcing before it belongs in the angle.
